chapters.title: Chapter 4: Building a Simple Pairs Trade

lessons.title: Entry and Exit Rules: Turning a Z-Score Into Buy/Sell Decisions

children.text: Lesson 7 turned a spread into a single comparable number, the z-score. Lesson 13 found candidate pairs worth trading. Neither one tells you, precisely, when to actually place an order and when to close it out. Without an explicit rule decided in advance, a trader ends up guessing in the moment, which is exactly when discipline tends to break down. This lesson turns the z-score into three concrete rules: when to enter, when to take profit, and when to cut losses.

body.text: A pairs trade needs three rules fixed before you enter, not decided in the moment: an entry threshold, a profit-taking exit, and a stop-loss. All three should be numbers you commit to in advance, based on the z-score, not a feeling about how the trade is going.

children.text: Lesson 7 already covered the sign convention. A z-score above a chosen positive threshold, commonly +2, means the spread is unusually high, the setup for shorting the spread. A z-score below the corresponding negative threshold, commonly -2, means the spread is unusually low, the setup for going long the spread. The exact threshold is a judgment call: a lower threshold like 1.5 enters more often but on weaker signals, a higher one like 2.5 enters less often but on stronger ones, and it should be set with the pair's own history and half-life (Lesson 3) in mind, not copied blindly from another pair.

cells: Short the spread: short the numerator stock, long the denominator stock, in the fitted hedge ratio
Long the spread: long the numerator stock, short the denominator stock, in the fitted hedge ratio
No entry; the spread is within its normal range

children.text: The Exit Rule: Taking Profit on Reversion

The natural exit is when the z-score reverts back toward zero, the spread returning to its historical average. In practice, waiting for an exact zero rarely works cleanly with noisy real data, so most rules use a small band instead, commonly exiting once |z| falls below something like 0.5, rather than holding out for a perfect return to the mean and giving back gains while waiting.
Worked Example: A Trade That Works as Planned

Continuing Lesson 7's spread series, the entry mean and standard deviation, 0.105 and 2.132, from the 19 days before entry, are frozen at the moment of entry and used for the rest of the trade, rather than constantly recalculated as new days come in. Day 20's z-score of about +2.30 triggers the entry rule: short the spread. Here is how the following days play out.

body.context: Day 20 entry to Day 24 exit, consistent with the fast, days-to-weeks half-life Lesson 3 described as the practically tradeable range.

body.text: Notice the trade did not wait for the z-score to hit exactly zero. It exited at -0.05, comfortably inside the ±0.5 band, on Day 24. Holding out for a perfect zero would have meant giving up a clean exit for an uncertain, possibly worse one later.

children.text: The Stop-Loss Rule: When the Thesis Isn't Playing Out

Not every trade reverts on schedule. A stop-loss needs its own threshold, wider than the entry level, commonly something like ±3.5, so a spread that keeps widening after entry gets closed out before losses compound. A second, independent kind of stop is time-based: if the spread hasn't reverted within some multiple of its estimated half-life, say three times the half-life from Lesson 3, exit regardless of where the z-score sits, since a reversion that keeps not happening is itself information.
Worked Example: A Trade That Needs a Stop-Loss
Same entry, same Day 20 z-score of +2.30, short the spread. This time the spread does not cooperate.

body.caption: Z-score path after entry, a widening scenario (illustrative)

cells: Stop-loss: exceeds the +3.5 threshold, exit at a loss

body.text: A stop-loss triggering is not just bad luck to shrug off. A spread that keeps widening instead of reverting is exactly the pattern Lesson 4 and Lesson 8 described as worth investigating for a structural break, and Lesson 11's cointegration test is worth re-running on updated data before considering re-entering the same pair.

body.title: Find the spread value at the exit band
body.prompt: Using the frozen entry mean of 0.105 and standard deviation of 2.132 from this lesson's worked example, what raw spread value corresponds to exactly a z-score of 0.5?
body.explanation: Spread = mean + z × std = 0.105 + 0.5 × 2.132 ≈ 1.17. Any spread value at or below this, moving toward the mean from an initial positive entry, would fall inside the ±0.5 exit band.

body.title: Hold, exit, or stop out?
body.question: A pair was entered short at z = +2.4. Three days later, the z-score reads +3.6, using the same frozen entry statistics, and the stop-loss threshold is set at ±3.5. What should happen?
options: Hold, since the spread is still positive and might revert soon
Exit at the stop-loss; the z-score has moved further against the position, past the stop-loss threshold
Add to the position, since a more extreme z-score means an even better entry
Do nothing until the z-score returns to exactly zero
body.explanation: A z-score of +3.6 exceeds the +3.5 stop-loss threshold, meaning the spread has widened further against the position rather than reverting. The stop-loss rule exists precisely to close the trade at this point rather than hoping it turns around.

body.title: Entry and Exit Rules: Core Terms

cards.definition: The z-score level, commonly around ±2, at which a pairs trade is opened, betting on reversion toward the mean.
Closing a position once the z-score has reverted close enough to zero, commonly within a small band like ±0.5, rather than waiting for an exact return to the mean.
A z-score level wider than the entry threshold, commonly around ±3.5, at which a losing position is closed to prevent further losses if the spread keeps widening.

An exit rule based on how long a position has been held rather than the z-score alone, commonly some multiple of the spread's estimated half-life, used when reversion simply isn't happening on schedule.

points: A pairs trade needs three rules fixed in advance: an entry threshold, a profit-taking exit, and a stop-loss, not decisions made in the moment.
A common entry rule is |z| ≥ 2, with the direction set by the sign: positive z shorts the spread, negative z goes long the spread.
Profit-taking exits typically use a small band around zero, like |z| ≤ 0.5, rather than waiting for an exact return to the mean.

A stop-loss threshold, wider than the entry level, closes a losing position before further widening compounds the loss. A time-based stop, tied to the spread's half-life from Lesson 3, catches trades that simply aren't reverting on schedule.
A triggered stop-loss is information, not just bad luck. It is worth checking for the kind of structural break Lessons 4, 8, and 11 discussed before re-entering the same pair.
